title: Navigation without a compass
summary: Find direction from a shadow stick, an analog watch or the night sky, and stay on course.

steps: Push a straight stick upright into level ground where it casts a clear shadow, and mark the tip of its shadow. This first mark is always west.
Wait at least 15 minutes, until the tip has moved a few inches, and mark the new shadow tip.
A line from the first mark to the second runs roughly west to east. Stand with the first mark on your left and the second on your right, and you’re facing north.

blocks.cap: The first mark is always west. The line it gives is only approximate.

list: Northern Hemisphere: hold the watch flat and point the hour hand at the sun. South is halfway between the hour hand and 12 o’clock. During daylight saving time, use 1 o’clock instead of 12.

blocks.cap: A rough method. It can be in error, more so the closer you are to the equator, and following it can lead you in circles.

list: North Star: follow the two stars at the outer edge of the Big Dipper’s cup about five times the gap between them. Polaris is less than a degree from true north, and its height above the horizon roughly equals your latitude.

blocks.cap: The Big Dipper turns around Polaris through the night. Its two pointer stars still point to it.

list: Moon: if it rises before the sun sets, its lit side faces west. If it rises after midnight, the lit side faces east. Use this only as a rough check.

Pace count: count each time the same foot lands. Learn how many paces you take per 100 m by walking a measured course several times and taking the average. Your count changes on slopes and on sand, mud or snow, and it only ever gives an approximate distance.
Pick a landmark on your line of travel, as far ahead as you can see, walk to it, then pick the next. Choose them as you go.
Follow handrails like streams, ridges and roads, and pick a catching feature past your goal so you know when you’ve overshot.
Aim off: to hit a spot on a river, aim deliberately to one side, by about 10 degrees, so you know which way to turn when you reach it.

blocks.cap: Small errors add up over distance. Aiming off tells you which way to turn when you reach the river.

blocks.p: To see how much daylight is left, check today’s sunset and last light in the Daylight and moon tool.

sources.name: US Army TC 3-25.26, Map Reading and Land Navigation (November 2013), chapters 5 and 8
sources.used: Shadow-tip method: wait 10 to 15 minutes until the tip moves a few inches, first mark always west everywhere on earth (8-17, 8-18); watch method: north temperate zone only, hour hand at the sun, south midway to 12, 1 o'clock on daylight saving time (8-19), can be in error especially at lower latitudes and may cause circling (8-21); North Star less than 1 degree off true north, pointer stars five times their distance (8-24); a pace is one natural step, count paces over a measured course (5-20); deliberate offset, about ten degrees (8-15)

sources.name: US Army FM 21-76, Survival Manual, chapter 18 (pp. 194-198)
sources.used: Shadow-tip steps in order: level spot, clear shadow, first mark always west, wait 10 to 15 minutes, approximate east-west line, first mark on your left and second on your right to face north; watch method: hold the watch horizontal, hour hand at the sun, bisect to 12, 1 o'clock on daylight saving time, more accurate farther from the equator; moon lit side west if it rises before sunset, east if after midnight; pointer stars at the outer lip of the Big Dipper, extend about five times; the Big Dipper rotates around Polaris

sources.name: US Army ATP 3-50.21, Survival (September 2018), chapter 7
sources.used: A pace is the distance covered every time the same foot touches the ground; establish it by pacing a measured course many times and averaging; slopes and surfaces such as sand, mud and snow change it; pace counts give only approximate distances (7-83); errors compound over distance (7-52); steering marks chosen as you move, the most distant object along the line of march (7-55); deliberate offset of about 10 degrees to a linear feature such as a road, ridge or stream, then turn in the direction of the offset (7-58); North Star height matches latitude (7-33, 7-35)

sources.name: StarDate (University of Texas McDonald Observatory), Directions, 18 September 2021
sources.used: Pointer stars Merak and Dubhe at the outer edge of the Big Dipper's bowl point to Polaris; Polaris's height above the horizon corresponds to your latitude

sources.name: Orienteering Ireland, Skills and Techniques in Orienteering
sources.used: Handrails are linear features you follow; a catching feature beyond the control tells you that you have gone too far; aiming off to one side tells you which way to turn
